title: Tendinitis and the accumulation model
summary: A guide to tendinitis and the author's tendon accumulation model, explaining persistent pain, proposed cellular mechanisms, and recurrent symptoms. It presents a hypotoxic diet, hydration, gentle rehabilitation, and lifestyle measures as parts of Family Clinic's integrated approach.

blocks.text: 1. Foreword

Tendinitis is one of the most common musculoskeletal conditions, affecting both athletes and people exposed to repetitive movements in their professional or everyday lives. It is a major reason for consultations in rheumatology and sports medicine. Yet behind this generic term lies a much more complex reality: not all forms of tendinitis are identical. Some disappear with rest or physiotherapy, while others resist treatment, recur, and become chronic, sometimes disabling.

This booklet aims to give the general public a clear understanding of the mechanism of tendon accumulation, drawing on Dr. Seignalet's work and clinical experience gathered at Family Clinic. It offers a new interpretation of tendon pain by showing that diet and lifestyle play a decisive role in prevention and healing.

Beyond purely symptomatic treatments, this approach highlights a comprehensive strategy: reduce intake of harmful molecules, restore tendon flexibility, and return patients' freedom of movement. It fits an integrative view of health in which the body is considered an interdependent system: what happens in the intestine or metabolism affects joints, muscles, and tendons.

Chronic tendinitis is therefore not an inevitable fate. It often reflects a profound metabolic imbalance linked to an unsuitable diet, poor waste elimination, or silent inflammation. Understanding this link between nutrition and pain is essential for effective action.

This document is part of Family Clinic's mission: offer practical, educational, scientifically grounded tools to support everyone toward better health. It addresses athletes and sedentary people alike, healthcare professionals and patients wishing to understand their body.
At Family Clinic, we believe knowledge is the first step toward healing: understanding the cause of pain makes it possible to overcome it durably.
2. Understanding tendinitis

Tendinitis is among the most common conditions in rheumatology. It affects athletes, but also people who perform repetitive movements at work or in everyday life. The tendon, the fibrous cord connecting muscle to bone, is essential for transmitting force and enabling movement. When healthy, it provides flexibility and power. But when weakened, it becomes painful and severely limits activity.
Three major types of tendinitis are distinguished:

items: Traumatic: linked to sudden exertion or mechanical overload.
Microtraumatic: caused by repeated movements or prolonged postures.
Metabolic or accumulation-related: without an apparent cause, often bilateral or migrating, reflecting altered tendon metabolism.

blocks.text: Accumulation-related tendinitis is the most puzzling. It does not respond to conventional treatments and frequently recurs. It reflects a deeper problem: disrupted cellular functioning.

At Family Clinic, we regularly see patients with chronic tendinitis. Many have already tried medications, local injections, or physiotherapy without lasting success. Our integrative approach, based on hypotoxic nutrition and prevention, offers them a new perspective.

We explain that tendon pain is more than mechanical: it often reflects a metabolic disorder. The tendon, poorly nourished or burdened with waste, loses flexibility and regenerative capacity. This phenomenon is comparable to a clogged engine: as long as impurities are not eliminated, function remains impaired.
Understanding your pain is the first step toward relieving it. At Family Clinic, we help you identify underlying causes and restore tendon health.
3. The accumulation mechanism

The accumulation theory developed by Dr. Seignalet explains why some forms of tendinitis become chronic. In the small intestine, certain poorly digested dietary and bacterial molecules enter the blood. They then deposit in tissues, particularly tendons.
Tenocytes, the cells responsible for producing collagen and elastin, become burdened by this waste. The result:

items: Reduced production of quality fibers.
A thickened, stiff, painful tendon.
Absence of conventional inflammation, resulting in normal laboratory tests.

blocks.text: This mechanism explains why anti-inflammatory drugs or local injections provide only temporary relief. They do not address the cause: accumulation of harmful molecules in the tendon.

Tendon accumulation is therefore a silent, metabolic, progressive disease process. It develops slowly, often quietly, until causing persistent pain. The most heavily used tendons — shoulder, elbow, knee, ankle — are affected first.

At Family Clinic, we explain this process to patients through simple diagrams and educational booklets. Understanding the true cause of pain helps them accept a different treatment based on diet and lifestyle.
The key is not to calm pain but to purify the underlying environment. This is how the tendon regains flexibility and function.
4. Symptoms and disease course

Accumulation-related tendinitis is distinguished by its insidious nature and resistance to conventional treatments. It does not always manifest through visible inflammation but through persistent, often migrating pain that eventually limits the simplest everyday movements. Unlike traumatic tendinitis, it is not linked to an impact or a single episode of overload: it develops gradually, reflecting a profound metabolic disorder.
The most frequent symptoms are:

items: Sharp, localized pain triggered by movement or muscle contraction.
Morning stiffness, with a feeling of a ‘rusty’ or numb tendon.
Persistent, sometimes fluctuating discomfort that may migrate from one joint to another.
Improvement with rest, but rapid relapse when activity resumes.
Absence of conventional inflammatory signs, often resulting in normal laboratory tests.

blocks.text: These forms of tendinitis can affect all attachment sites:

items: Shoulder: involvement of the supraspinatus or long head of the biceps, causing pain when raising the arm.
Elbow: lateral or medial epicondylitis, typical of repetitive movements.
Knee: patellar tendinitis, common in runners and jumpers.
Ankle: Achilles tendon involvement, often bilateral.
Hip: gluteus medius or trochanteric tendinitis, interfering with walking and sleep.

blocks.text: Their course is slow, unpredictable, and recurrent. Conventional treatments — anti-inflammatory drugs, local injections, physiotherapy — provide partial relief but do not prevent recurrence. Many patients describe temporary improvement followed by relapse as soon as sport or work resumes. This cyclical pattern reflects persistence of the underlying accumulation state, uncorrected by symptomatic approaches.

From a laboratory perspective, accumulation-related tendinitis lacks the usual inflammatory markers: CRP and ESR remain normal; ultrasound sometimes shows tendon thickening without rupture or calcification. This paradox — intense pain without apparent inflammation — long puzzled clinicians before the accumulation theory offered a coherent explanation.

The tendon, saturated with foreign molecules, loses flexibility and its ability to glide. Collagen fibers become stiff and poorly hydrated and develop cracks under exertion. This process comes with altered local microcirculation: nourishing capillaries become blocked, cellular exchanges slow, and repair becomes impossible.

At Family Clinic, we observe that these forms of tendinitis often come with other signs of accumulation: chronic fatigue, widespread pain, digestive disturbances, joint stiffness, or muscular hypersensitivity. They form part of an overall syndrome of metabolic accumulation in which the tendon is just one target organ among others.

Management must therefore be comprehensive. Treating the tendon is insufficient: the underlying environment must be purified. This requires a suitable diet, adequate hydration, gentle regular physical activity, and stress management. Deep massage, progressive stretching, and local treatments can support healing, but their effectiveness depends on the quality of the internal environment.
At Family Clinic, we offer personalized monitoring:

items: Complete assessment to identify sources of accumulation.
Dietary advice adapted to the patient's profile.
A gentle rehabilitation program to restore mobility without worsening pain.
Regular monitoring to adjust the protocol and prevent relapses.

blocks.text: We know chronic pain isolates and discourages. This is why our approach combines education with human support. Understanding the mechanism of tendinitis already means regaining control.
Family Clinic reminds us that chronic tendinitis is not an inevitable fate: by acting on the metabolic cause, it is possible to restore tendon flexibility and vitality.
5. The role of the hypotoxic diet

The hypotoxic diet developed by Dr. Seignalet is an innovative nutritional approach aiming to reduce intake of harmful molecules responsible for metabolic accumulation. It rests on a simple observation: our modern diet, rich in mutated cereal grains, dairy products, and harsh cooking methods, generates protein fragments and toxins that the body struggles to eliminate. These molecules cross the intestinal barrier, circulate in the blood, and deposit in tissues, particularly tendons.

By eliminating certain modern foods and favoring natural products, raw or cooked at low temperatures, the hypotoxic diet restores intestinal permeability and reduces deposits in tendons. It thus acts directly on the cause of chronic tendinitis: cellular accumulation.
The observed results are encouraging:

items: Complete disappearance of pain in many patients, sometimes within weeks.
Marked improvement in flexibility and recovery, allowing physical activity to resume without fear of relapse.
A significant reduction in long-term recurrences, confirming that dietary modification acts on the underlying metabolic state.
Stabilization of benefits after a few months, with lasting improvement as long as the diet is followed.

blocks.text: Conversely, abandoning the diet almost always causes relapse, confirming the direct link between diet and accumulation. This observation is fundamental: it shows that chronic tendinitis is not an inevitable fate but the consequence of an imbalance that can be corrected.
The hypotoxic diet is more than a list of prohibitions. It offers true dietary retraining:

items: Replace mutated cereal grains (modern wheat, industrial corn) with more easily digested alternatives such as basmati rice, quinoa, or buckwheat.
Eliminate animal dairy products, often responsible for immune reactions, and favor plant milks (almond, coconut, oat).
Avoid harsh cooking methods (grilling, frying, high-temperature ovens) that denature proteins and generate toxic molecules.
Favor raw foods or foods gently steamed, preserving enzymes and essential nutrients.
Include fresh fruit and vegetables rich in antioxidants to support detoxification and cellular regeneration.

blocks.text: At Family Clinic, we have incorporated this diet into our protocols. We support patients through dietary transition with simple recipes, practical booklets, and medical monitoring. We know changing habits can seem difficult: this is why we provide step-by-step support adapted to cultural and local constraints.

The hypotoxic diet is not limited to tendinitis. It acts on a range of chronic conditions: osteoarthritis, polyarthritis, colitis, migraines, and chronic fatigue. For tendinitis, it offers a concrete solution to restore tendon flexibility and return patients' freedom of movement.
Family Clinic reminds us that hypotoxic nutrition is not a panacea but a complementary strategy addressing the underlying cause of chronic tendinitis: metabolic accumulation.
6. Synthesis and prevention

Tendinitis is common, but its accumulation mechanism explains why some forms become chronic and resistant to conventional treatments. Understanding this reality transforms management: rather than masking pain with anti-inflammatory drugs or local injections, the aim is to address the underlying cause, namely buildup of harmful molecules in tendons.
Prevention relies on a comprehensive approach incorporating several dimensions:

items: Hypotoxic diet: reduce mutated cereal grains, dairy products, and harsh cooking methods; favor raw or steamed plant foods to limit metabolic waste accumulation.
Adequate hydration: regularly drink quality water to promote toxin elimination and maintain tissue flexibility.
Gentle, regular stretching: preserve joint mobility and tendon flexibility, avoid morning stiffness, and improve local circulation.
Suitable physical activity: practice moderate sport, avoid repetitive movements or mechanical overload, and favor gradual progression and recovery.
Lifestyle: manage stress, improve sleep, and avoid toxic substances (tobacco, alcohol) that worsen metabolic accumulation.

blocks.text: This new perspective transforms management: the tendon is no longer considered a simple mechanical structure but a living tissue sensitive to the metabolic environment. By purifying the underlying environment, function is restored and patients regain freedom of movement.

Accumulation-related tendinitis often signals a broader disorder: it comes with widespread pain, chronic fatigue, or digestive or joint disturbances. It should therefore be interpreted as an alarm signal: the body expresses an overload it can no longer eliminate. Acting early helps avoid progression to more serious conditions such as osteoarthritis or autoimmune diseases.

At Family Clinic, we believe health comes through understanding and prevention. Our booklets, consultations, and practical workshops are designed to help everyone regain control of their health. We support patients step by step, giving them concrete tools: hypotoxic recipes, stretching programs, and personalized advice.

Preventing chronic tendinitis requires everyday discipline but offers considerable benefits: disappearance of pain, improved mobility, renewed energy, and better quality of life. It gives patients back the possibility of pursuing activities without fear, regaining confidence in their body, and escaping the vicious circle of pain and recurrence.

Family Clinic reminds us that chronic tendinitis is not an inevitable fate. By acting on diet, lifestyle, and prevention, it is possible to restore tendon health and regain an active, fulfilling life.
